title: Edges and endings
summary: Off-by-one errors, choosing while or for, and making sure every loop ends. Delve gets its game loop: read a command, play a turn, stop for the right reason.

steps.title: Off by one
body: The most common loop bug in every language is running **one time too many or too few**. Ask two questions of every loop:
- What is the **first** value the counter takes?
- What is the **last**?
```text
for (i = 0; i < 5; i++)     0 1 2 3 4     five passes
for (i = 0; i <= 5; i++)    0 1 2 3 4 5   six passes
for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++)    1 2 3 4 5     five passes
Python range(0, 5)          0 1 2 3 4     the end is excluded
Arrays start at index 0, so an array of length `n` has its last item at `n - 1`. The loop `i < n` fits it exactly; `i <= n` reads one past the end and crashes.

steps.prompt: How many times does each loop body run?
steps.explain: A loop from `a` up to but not including `b` runs `b - a` times. Include the end and it runs one more.

steps.prompt: Fence posts: a 10 metre fence with a post every 2 metres. What is printed?
steps.explain: Posts at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10: six posts for five gaps. This *fencepost error* is where off-by-one gets its other name.

steps.title: while or for?
body: Both repeat. They suit different questions:
- `for` when you know **how many** times, or are walking a range or collection.
- `while` when you repeat **until something happens** and cannot tell in advance how long it takes.

A `while` loop only stops if its body changes something the condition reads. Each pass must make **progress** towards making the condition false. If nothing in the loop moves closer to the exit, it is an **infinite loop**.
Below, `n` halves every pass, so it must eventually reach 1. That shrinking quantity is the proof the loop ends.

steps.prompt: Will each loop finish, or run forever?
steps.explain: `10, 7, 4, 1, -2, ...` skips straight past 0, so `!= 0` never becomes false. Prefer `>` or `<` over `!=` in loop conditions: they survive jumps.

steps.title: break and continue
body: Two keywords bend a loop, and they exist in C#, Java, Python and JavaScript alike:
- `continue` skips the **rest of this pass** and moves on to the next one.
- `break` leaves the loop **entirely**.
Use `break` when you have found what you were looking for, and `continue` to skip items that do not interest you without wrapping the whole body in an `if`.

steps.explain: 3 is added, -1 skipped, 4 added, -5 skipped, then 9 triggers `break` so 2 is never reached. 3 + 4 = 7.

steps.title: Fix the off-by-one
prompt: `SumRange(a, b)` should add every whole number from `a` to `b` **inclusive**. `SumRange(1, 4)` should be `10`, but it returns `6`. Fix it.
starter: for (int i = a; i < b; i++)
solution: for (int i = a; i <= b; i++)
hints: Which value of `i` is never added? Trace `SumRange(1, 4)` by hand.
The last pass should have `i == b`.

steps.title: Collatz steps
prompt: The Collatz rule: if `n` is even, halve it; if odd, make it `3n + 1`. Nobody has proved this always reaches 1, but it has for every number ever tried.
Write `int CollatzSteps(int n)` returning how many steps it takes to reach 1. `CollatzSteps(6)` is `8`: 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. `CollatzSteps(1)` is `0`.

require.message: Uses a while loop (the number of steps is not known in advance)

hints: You do not know how many steps in advance, so this is a `while (n != 1)` loop.
Inside: update `n` with the rule, then add one to a step counter.

steps.title: A loop that reads commands
body: A game is a loop: read a command, act on it, repeat. `Console.ReadLine()` reads one line typed by the player (without the Enter). When the input has **ended** (the player closed it, or a script of commands ran out) it returns `null` instead of a string, so its type is `string?`: a string *or nothing*.
```csharp
string? line = Console.ReadLine();
if (line == null) return "quit";       // no more input: leave, or this loop spins forever
string command = line.Trim().ToLower(); // " N " -> "n"

A loop like this has **several** ways to end, and every one must be written down: the input runs out, the player types `q`, something in the game ends it, or a limit is reached. Forget one and the program hangs. `continue` skips to the next pass without counting it: right for a blank line.

steps.title: Delve's game loop
prompt: Write **`static string GameLoop(int maxTurns)`**, the loop one Delve floor runs in. Each pass:
1. Read a line. If the input has ended (`null`), return `"quit"`.
2. Trim it and make it lower case. A blank command is skipped: it does **not** use up a turn.
4. Anything else is a turn: count it, then call **`Turn(command)`**, which plays it and returns `"ok"`, `"dead"` or `"descend"`. Anything other than `"ok"` ends the loop: return it.
When `maxTurns` turns have been played without the loop ending, the torch is out: return `"torch out"`.

`Turn` is Delve's engine. Here the checks supply a stand-in that prints `turn: <command>` and returns `"dead"` for `die` and `"descend"` for `>`; they feed your loop scripted input, as if a player typed it.

forbid.message: Every function starts with `static` (Delve keeps its pieces in one static class)
Calls Turn, does not write its own (the game has one)

hints: A `while (turns < maxTurns)` loop with `turns` counting only the commands passed to Turn. After the loop: `return "torch out";`.
Order inside the loop: read, null check, trim + lower, blank check (`continue`), `q` check, then `turns++` and `Turn(command)`.
The result of Turn decides everything: `if (result != "ok") return result;`

build.unlocks: Delve keeps going now: walk a whole floor, one command at a time, until you quit, fall or find the stairs.
